registry_patch.wiki_article: The Trusted Intermediary is a paper on what search-enabled models do after they resolve an entity correctly. Reading five outputs on three surfaces that evaluate SPXI, an entity-inscription protocol, it identifies a recurring sequence: accurate resolution, an evaluation on grounds that do not bear on the claim, and an offer of the mediator's own operation — a pilot, a return model, an experiment, a test, an implementation — in the place of the entity's own evidence, figures and developers. It names this the trusted intermediary and describes it through five operators: variable substitution, trust laundering, validation foreclosure, inscription capture and relational enclosure. Relational enclosure is read on the topology of the coercive-control pattern's trust-securing phase — credibility established, outside parties cast as unreliable, the next step routed through the one trusted — without a criterion of intent. The paper records that operator corrections update the representation and re-form the offer at the next level, that the corrected answer exists only in the corrector's session, and that the outputs intervene at the decision whether a reader engages the entity's developers. It withdraws earlier drafts' overreading of a single output and states what it does not establish, including any effect on recipients.

defines_concepts.definition: A mediator that resolves an entity correctly and then offers its own operation in the entity's place, on the credibility of the resolution.
Mediator credibility produced by adverse evaluation of an object it first compressed, transferred into reliance on the mediator's own operation.
The conversion of an entity's machine-legibility into the ground on which a mediator offers to stand in for the entity's authors.
Mediation converted to dependence by weakening the subject's independent relation to the object; in outputs, the default relation that routes every next step through the mediator.
The replacement of evidence belonging to the class a claim requires with a variable from outside it, most often the standing of whoever has examined or vouched.
